newsitem.title: JAPAN: Mark seen rising vs yen, but gains to be fleeting.
newsitem.headline: Mark seen rising vs yen, but gains to be fleeting.

text.p: The mark, battered recently by a rampaging dollar, may well gain a bit on the yen after taking heart from supportive comments by the German central bank.
But dealers and analysts here said rises are likely to be fleeting at best, citing fundamental economic factors and the likelihood of further mark weakening against the dollar.

"The mark is likely to try higher against the yen just once more, to around 75 yen. But I feel it's getting close to the top and that over the long term it will weaken," said Nobuya Shida, manager at the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan.

The German currency has perked up against both the yen and the dollar since Wednesday, when Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said he expected the normalisation of the mark's exchange rate against the dollar to end soon.

Buying ensued after the market interpreted this as a signal that a subtle change may have emerged in the stance of German monetary authorities, who have repeatedly said they had no problems with their currency's recent fall.

Although a British bank dealer said the comments gave players a sense that any new dollar forays over 1.65 marks were no longer welcome, tending to support the mark against both the dollar and yen, most in Tokyo felt the impact was temporary.

"We need some verification of the comments, or remarks from other German authorities, before we can see if this is a real change," said Long-Term Credit's Shida, who attributed the mark's rise on the yen to active investor bids, including some from life insurers, in connection with foreign bond buying.

He added that while the mark could slip to around 73.00 yen, it will remain within the 72.00-76.00 yen range of the past six months. It would take either "a substantial (downward) correction of the dollar on the yen" or an equally unlikely tightening of Japanese monetary policy to force it below 72.00 yen by the end of March, when Japan's fiscal year ends. Over the next two weeks, the mark will move from 72.00 to 75.00 yen, he said. It stood at 74.40/45 yen by midday on Friday.

Kenneth Landon, a senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said that while he expected the mark to have scope for a move up to 75.50 yen over the short term, end-March was likely to find it near 72.50 yen.

"We've been seeing some good mark strength against European currencies right now on recent expectations of a narrower EMU, with some fund shifts from the peseta and lira back to the mark," he added, noting that this was inviting buying of marks for yen from a range of players, including U.S. names.

European economic and monetary union (EMU), which will bring about the new "Euro" currency, is set to start in 1999, with member countries to be decided by the end of 1997 after assessment of a variety of criteria. Expectations of a "hard" Euro, with a relatively small group of participating countries, tend to buoy the mark.

A dealer with Dresdner Bank AG in Tokyo said that while it is difficult to predict the mark's long-term course until the situation with the Euro is clearer, he too feels it will be around 72.00 to 73.00 yen by end-March.
"Although we may see the mark try 75.00 yen soon, recent rises are more due to technical factors than anything else, meaning any gains will be short-lived," he added.

Even though the approaching end of Japan's fiscal year usually leads to a stronger yen, with Japanese operators selling foreign assets to repatriate funds for book-closing window dressing, dealers think this year will be different.

"We may be seeing some repatriation this year but not much, because most investors are thinking of increasing their weighting of foreign holdings. So if they (sell foreign assets to) take profits, they'll just get right back in again," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's Landon said.
